text: I’ll treat the 90 mm as the lateral distance from each plenum side to the port-face centreline. Each runner therefore has a 30 mm horizontal lead followed by a 90° downward bend of 60 mm centreline radius; its port face is horizontal. I’ll assume a 30 mm straight throttle neck because its length was not specified. The fluid will be a boolean union of the plenum, neck, and eight swept circular runners, then meshed initially with a coarse snappyHexMesh background grid. First I’m checking the installed CAD sweep interfaces needed for that construction.

The first probe found the sweep call but stopped on a nonexistent wire convenience method, so I will not rely on anything from that failed cell. I’m checking the algebra-mode line/arc constructors directly.

I’ll now build the coarse CAD fluid volume in metres. The four runner stations are an explicit assumption: 45, 115, 185, and 255 mm from the throttle-end plenum face (70 mm spacing and 45 mm end margins). The picture and measurements will verify the union, runner reach, bend angle/radius, and end-face locations before any mesh setup.

The attempted build exposed two concrete issues and is not suitable for replay: the rotated cylinder’s alignment placed the throttle neck away from the box (two solids), and my bend measurement selected the wrong path edge. I’ll rebuild the neck by explicit vector extrusion, inspect every path edge, and render directly through the installed off-screen backend.
The extrusion API takes a scalar along the profile plane normal, not a vector. I’ll correct only that call and rerun the self-contained coarse build.

The coarse shape is visibly correct and is one solid, but the path measurement reveals the bend created by `RadiusArc` is 88.34°, not the requested 90°. I will not accept that approximation. I’m inspecting the actual arc geometry and endpoints so I can replace it with an exact centre-defined quarter circle.

The inspection confirms why: the three-dimensional radius-arc constructor chose an unintended oblique circle (64.81 mm actual radius). I’ll use the low-level circle-edge constructor on an explicitly defined Y–Z plane to remove that ambiguity.
I’ll replace all eight bend paths with exact 90° circular edges whose local plane axes are defined explicitly. This cell updates the coarse fluid shape and repeats the measurements and preview.

The corrected preview shows all eight continuous runners and the throttle neck, and the requested bend is now exactly 90°. Next I’ll inspect the final union’s boundary faces to tag the throttle disk, eight port disks, plenum/neck walls, and runner walls from their actual CAD faces before the single coordinated patch export.

The union has exactly the expected 32 boundary faces: 8 planar port disks, 8 toroidal bend walls, 8 cylindrical runner lead walls, the throttle disk and neck cylinder, and 6 trimmed plenum faces. I’ll tag negative‑Y runners as `port_left_1..4`, positive‑Y as `port_right_1..4`, use all toroidal and runner-sized cylindrical faces for `runner_walls`, and assign the remaining box/neck faces to `plenum_walls`. Then I’ll export all patches in one seam-preserving call.

The coordinated export is watertight (0 open, flipped, or non-manifold edges). I’ll now create a deliberately coarse background mesh at roughly 8 mm spacing, apply one surface-refinement level (about 4 mm near the manifold boundary), and retain the interior point at the plenum centre. This should resolve a 38 mm runner with about 9–10 cells across near its wall without overbuilding the first mesh.
The dictionaries are ready for all 11 named surfaces. I’ll generate the background grid first and inspect its basic dimensions before surface conformation.
The background mesh has 33,660 cells at 7.65–8.0 mm spacing, as intended. I’ll now run snappyHexMesh in overwrite mode and inspect its final cell/patch summary.

snappyHexMesh did not start because this OpenFOAM build requires placeholder finite-volume dictionaries even for meshing. I’ll add minimal empty `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` files; no solver settings or boundary conditions are being introduced.
The required empty dictionaries are now present. I’ll rerun the surface-conforming mesh.
This release also validates the usual scheme subdictionaries. I’ll add only inert defaults required by the mesher (`none`/basic Gauss forms), still without any physical model or field boundary data.
The mesher prerequisites are complete; I’ll run snappyHexMesh again.
The conformed mesh completed with 37,405 cells (33,078 at the refined level) and no final snappy quality errors. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` now and inspect patch counts and topology.

The binding check passes: one connected region, all 11 requested boundary patches present, 37,405 cells, maximum non-orthogonality 43.64°, maximum skewness 1.71, and `Mesh OK`. I’ll make a surface rendering of the actual OpenFOAM mesh to verify that the patch layout and runner openings survived meshing.
The VTK conversion confirms every named patch was written from the actual mesh. I’ll render those mesh faces with distinct colors and visible cell edges for the final visual inspection.

Final visual inspection shows a continuous plenum and eight resolved curved runners; all ports remain separate mesh patches. The mesh and exports are complete, so I’m submitting the case checks with no expected advisory exceptions.

The advisory coverage check warned while simultaneously confirming that all 69,060 surface triangles are covered exactly once across the 11 patches. That is the intended complete, non-overlapping partition, so I’m explicitly waiving this informational warning and resubmitting.
